::: {.why}
A recurrent or attention model on a return series is looking for temporal structure, and week 6 already measured how much of that exists in returns as opposed to in their magnitudes.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Say what structure a sequence model can find that your engineered features cannot, and whether your data has it.
- Report a sequence model against the same baselines and interpret the result in terms of what week 6 measured.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [40 min]{.task-min} Fit a small sequence model on a window of past returns and volumes per name, under the same protocol. Report it against the baselines. Then run it on absolute returns as the target rather than signed returns, and note that it does far better, which is the same fact you measured on day 38 appearing in a different form.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Draw the conclusion for your book: the temporal structure in this data is mostly in volatility rather than in direction, so a sequence model is a good volatility forecaster and a poor return forecaster, and the right place for it is sizing rather than signal. Write that into the milestone.
:::
:::

A sequence model evaluated on signed and on absolute returns, with the conclusion about where its capacity actually pays.
:::

## Checkpoint

Your sequence model forecasts volatility well and direction badly. Which stylized fact predicted that?
:::
